title: Lesson 56: Kubernetes for Agents: Pods, Autoscaling, and GPU Scheduling
description: Packaging agents as pods managed by a Deployment, scaling them with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and KEDA event driven autoscaling, and routing self-hosted model inference to GPUs through device plugins and node placement.

questions.question: Why does scaling agent workers on CPU lag behind a queue-driven workload?
options: CPU metrics are unavailable unless a device plugin is installed
CPU rises only after work is already being processed
CPU-based scaling is disabled whenever a pod requests a GPU
The autoscaler only ever scales down on CPU, never up
questions.explanation: CPU is a lagging reflection of work already in flight. A burst of queued tasks does not raise CPU until workers process them, and an agent waiting on a model call sits idle in CPU terms while tasks wait.

questions.question: How does event-driven autoscaling relate to the built-in pod autoscaler?
options: It extends the built-in autoscaler with external queue metrics
It replaces the built-in autoscaler, which must then be removed
It sets node taints so agent pods land on GPU nodes
It scales only on CPU and memory and never reads event sources
questions.explanation: Event-driven autoscaling works alongside the built-in autoscaler rather than replacing it. It feeds external metrics such as queue depth, and its operator handles scaling between zero and one replica of an idle workload.

questions.question: How does a pod request a GPU exposed as an extended resource?
options: In the requests field, so the GPU can be shared and overcommitted
In a separate plugin spec that bypasses the resource block
In the limits field, because the limit satisfies the request
In both fields, with requests set larger than limits
questions.explanation: For an extended resource the limit is what Kubernetes uses to satisfy the request, so a GPU is declared in the limits field. These resources are integer-only and cannot be overcommitted or shared between containers.
